pages.x: In 1980 workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, led by an electrician named Lech Wałęsa, went on strike and won the right to form Solidarity, the first free trade union in the Soviet bloc. Ten million Poles joined. The government crushed it under martial law in 1981, but it lived on underground, with the support of the Polish pope, John Paul II.

Soviet tanks had crushed every earlier revolt in Eastern Europe: East Germany in 1953, Hungary in 1956, Czechoslovakia in 1968. Mikhail Gorbachev made it clear that this time they would not come. His spokesman joked that the old rule had given way to the Sinatra Doctrine: each country could now do it its way.

Early in 1989 Poland's communists, with the economy in ruins, sat down with Solidarity at a round table and agreed to a partly free election. On 4 June, the day the tanks rolled into Tiananmen Square, Solidarity won all but one of the seats it was allowed to fight. By September Poland had a non-communist prime minister, the first in the Soviet bloc in forty years.

In May Hungary began cutting down the barbed-wire fence on its border with Austria. In August, at a picnic for peace on the border, a gate was opened for a few hours, and hundreds of East Germans on holiday ran through it to the West. In September Hungary opened the border for good, and tens of thousands followed.

In East Germany crowds marched every Monday in Leipzig, chanting we are the people. On 9 November a muddled official announced on live television that East Germans could travel freely, starting at once. That night thousands surged to the Berlin Wall, the guards opened the gates, and Berliners from both sides danced on top of it.

In Prague police beat up a student march on 17 November. Within days hundreds of thousands filled Wenceslas Square each evening, jingling their keys to tell the communists it was time to go. Václav Havel, a playwright jailed again and again for his writing, led the protests. By the end of December he was president.

Only in Romania was the end bloody. On 21 December the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu spoke to a crowd in Bucharest, and it began to boo him, live on television. The next day he fled by helicopter but was caught, and on Christmas Day he and his wife Elena were tried in less than an hour and shot. Over a thousand people died in the fighting.

In one year the communist rule that Soviet tanks had imposed on Eastern Europe after 1945 fell apart, almost without bloodshed. Germany was reunited in 1990, and within two years the Soviet Union itself was gone. Most of the countries freed in 1989 later joined the European Union and NATO.
pts: The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November
Six communist governments fell in a year
